lipolysis.def: The hydrolysis of stored triglycerides into glycerol and fatty acids inside fat cells. Epinephrine, norepinephrine, cortisol and growth hormone switch it on; insulin switches it off.

beta-oxidation.def: The breakdown of a fatty acid inside mitochondria, two carbons at a time, into acetyl CoA; each turn also makes one FADH2 and one NADH. It needs oxygen, because the carriers must be reoxidized by the electron transport chain.
roots: second letter of the Greek alphabet: the carbon being oxidized

ketogenesis.def: The liver's conversion of excess acetyl CoA into ketone bodies (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and a little acetone), which other tissues burn. A raised blood level is ketosis; enough to acidify the blood is ketoacidosis.

lipogenesis.def: The building of fatty acids and triglycerides from acetyl CoA, mainly in the liver and adipose tissue when fuel is plentiful and insulin is high.

lipoproteins.def: Particles that carry lipids in the blood: a core of triglycerides and cholesterol inside a shell of phospholipids and apolipoproteins. VLDL carries liver-made triglycerides, which lipoprotein lipase unloads into tissues; LDL carries cholesterol to cells; HDL returns cholesterol to the liver.

amino-acid-metabolism.def: The handling of amino acids beyond protein building. Transamination moves each amino group onto glutamate; deamination in the liver releases it as ammonia; the carbon skeleton is burned or made into glucose (glucogenic amino acids) or into ketone bodies or fat (ketogenic amino acids).

urea-cycle.def: A loop of reactions in liver cells that combines ammonia, bicarbonate and a nitrogen from aspartate into urea, spending 3 ATP per urea. Urea is far less toxic than ammonia and is excreted by the kidneys.
